title: A Four Step Process for End Users to Leverage Quantum Technology - Quantum Computing Report
gist: Doug Finke lays out Global Quantum Intelligence's four-step adoption framework — Discover, Decide, Execute, Incorporate — for enterprise managers evaluating quantum computing, with an explicit ROI gate that rejects quantum whenever a classical solution is equally good. His practical guidance (toy models first, multi-vendor benchmarking, Qiskit portability, integration as the hardest step) reveals where enterprise quantum spending actually goes and why deployment, not algorithms, is the bottleneck.

insights.claim: Global Quantum Intelligence proposes a four-step enterprise adoption sequence — Discover, Decide, Execute, Incorporate — as the path from curiosity to deployment for quantum technology, treating adoption as a staged program rather than a single pilot.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: A staged framework implies enterprise quantum revenue arrives as a long sequence of small consulting and machine-time purchases, not lumpy hardware sales — relevant to how vendors' revenue mixes will look.
insights.quote: a sequence we call Discover, Decide, Execute, Incorporate
insights.locator: To help guide users through this quandary

insights.claim: Discovery should start inward, interviewing colleagues about computational problems with excessively long run times, inaccurate results, or that are impossible on current infrastructure, and reviewing existing compute usage for unusually long-runtime applications.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Existing long-runtime classical workloads are the practical prospecting list for quantum vendors; industries with those profiles are the earliest realistic buyers.
insights.quote: ask about any computational problems that have excessively long run times, produce inaccurate results, or are not possible with your current computing environment

insights.claim: Users should get familiar with the different computing modalities and their strengths and weaknesses before selecting vendors, implying modality choice is an end-user decision rather than something the market has settled.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: No modality has won; a portfolio rather than a single-platform bet remains the rational exposure to quantum hardware.

themes.theme: The ROI gate and honest scoping

insights.claim: The explicit decision rule is that if a classical solution can provide an equally good result, a quantum solution probably is not worth building, and if benefits do not justify quantum-related expenses the project should be dropped.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: A quantum industry insider publishing a classical-first veto rule is a sober signal on realistic near-term TAM; discount vendor use-case counts that never apply this filter.
insights.quote: If a classical solution can provide an equally good solution, then it probably isn’t worth creating a quantum solution.

insights.claim: Project budgeting for quantum must cover manpower, software license fees, and machine time as distinct cost lines — machine time being a recurring operating expense unfamiliar to most enterprise IT planning.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Machine time and license fees, not hardware purchases, are where early enterprise quantum dollars land — supporting cloud-access and software business models over on-prem sales.

insights.claim: Enterprises face a build-versus-buy fork between creating an in-house innovation team and hiring external technical consultants to develop the quantum solution.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: The consultant path is the default for most enterprises given talent scarcity, which makes quantum services firms an earlier-revenue exposure than hardware makers.

insights.claim: Any plan requires performance, cost, and compatibility assessments including how the quantum application fits the rest of the organization's IT systems, before it goes to management for approval.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Compatibility assessment at the planning stage means quantum sales cycles are gated by enterprise architecture review, extending time-to-revenue for vendors.

insights.claim: Projects should begin with a toy model — the same problem with fewer data elements — to test the algorithm while reducing machine time charges and getting faster feedback.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Machine-time cost is high enough to shape methodology, which caps how much revenue vendors can extract from early-stage enterprise experimentation.
insights.quote: start out with a “toy” model that you can use to test out the proof of concept

insights.claim: Switching between quantum platforms is often possible with a single line of code change, and most hardware platforms accept or translate programs written in Qiskit.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Low switching costs mean quantum hardware vendors have weak software lock-in and will compete largely on price and performance — a margin warning for hardware names.
insights.quote: Often, it is possible to change to a different platform by a simple change in one line of code. And most hardware platforms can accept or translate programs written in Qiskit.

insights.claim: Different quantum platforms trade off distinct attributes — some have faster gate speeds while others have higher qubit fidelities — so users should benchmark several providers before committing.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Application-dependent platform fit means no single spec (qubit count, fidelity) determines commercial win rates; watch which workloads each vendor actually captures.
insights.quote: Some have faster gate speeds while others have higher qubit fidelities.

insights.claim: Synthetic data is recommended for testing quantum solutions where confidentiality is required, indicating data-governance constraints are a real friction in enterprise quantum pilots.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Confidentiality friction favors on-premises or sovereign quantum deployments in regulated sectors over shared cloud access.

insights.claim: Contrary to intuition, having a working quantum solution does not make production deployment easy — integrating it with the rest of the IT system often requires substantial detailed work.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: The gap between successful proof-of-concept announcements and production revenue is wider than press releases imply; discount POC news as a revenue signal.
insights.quote: Some may think that once you have in hand a working solution, putting it into production will be easy. In fact, the opposite is often true.

insights.claim: Organizational adoption requires additional documentation and training effort for staff not involved in development, making change management a distinct cost line in quantum deployment.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Training and documentation overhead lengthens payback periods and creates a services attach opportunity around quantum deployments.

insights.claim: Pre-production testing should deliberately construct unusual corner cases — scenarios unlikely in normal production but possible — to observe how the quantum solution behaves.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Probabilistic quantum outputs make edge-case behavior a genuine reliability risk, which is why regulated industries will adopt more slowly than enthusiasm suggests.

insights.claim: Global Quantum Intelligence's stated view is that immense economic value will accrue to end users of quantum technology, but identifying where it applies within a specific organization is not obvious.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: If value accrues to users rather than vendors, the quantum trade may be long adopting industries rather than long pure-play quantum stocks.
insights.quote: Global Quantum Intelligence (GQI) believes there will be immense economic value that will be enjoyed by end users of the technology
insights.locator: You may be a manager in a large enterprise

insights.claim: End users that start working with quantum technology early will likely obtain the greatest benefits, but the recommended entry is a small, well-planned program rather than a large team rushed into place.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Advocating small, staged entry implies enterprise quantum budgets stay modest near-term — a check on aggressive commercial revenue forecasts for the sector.
insights.quote: Those end users that start working with the technology early will likely obtain the greatest benefits.
